I've had my 8-inch Dobsonian for a little over two years now, and I finally feel like I'm past the frustrating fumbling-around stage. Star-hopping to the brighter Messier targets doesn't require a printed chart anymore; I can get from Polaris to M81 and M82 using naked-eye guide stars alone, and on a clear night I can usually track down six or seven deep-sky objects before my eyes start giving out. Saturn's rings and the Cassini division show up crisply once the scope's had time to cool down to ambient temperature, which took me embarrassingly long to figure out was even a thing I needed to do.

Lately I've been spending more time comparing eyepieces than actually observing, if I'm honest. My old 25mm Plossl does fine for wide fields, but I picked up a 10mm wide-angle a few months back and the extra apparent field makes a real difference on planetary detail. I still collimate with a basic Cheshire rather than a laser, mostly because I want to get faster and more consistent at doing it by eye before I add another gadget to the routine. Averted vision for faint fuzzies like the Ring Nebula is finally starting to click instead of feeling like a party trick I got lucky with.

My next project is dialing in polar alignment well enough to try some short tracked exposures with my phone held up to the eyepiece, just to see what I can pull out of a light-polluted sky before I consider anything more serious.

I keep fish tank more than twenty years now, since I was young man in my country before I move here. Now I have six tanks in my basement, three for breeding the rams and two apisto species that are not so easy, one just for growing out fry until they are big enough to sell to local shop.

Every month the beginner club in my city ask me to come and explain the nitrogen cycle to new members, because many people buy fish same day like the tank and then wonder why everybody die in one week. I try explain slow and simple because I remember when I was also confuse about this many years ago.

Last year I am judge for the small aquascaping contest at the pet expo, this was first time and I was very nervous but the other judges say my notes on the hardscape balance were most detailed of all three judges, ha. My water parameters I do not even test so much anymore because after all this years I know just from looking at the plants and the fish behavior if something is wrong, small things like the tetras staying near the top too much tell me oxygen is maybe low before test kit even show number.

Right now my project is trying to breed the more difficult killifish species, this one is giving me trouble because the eggs need dry period and I still learning best humidity for the peat moss. Even after so many years there is still something new to learn, this is why I still love this hobby so much.

My last three all-grain batches have all finished two or three points higher than my recipe software predicted, so this weekend I'm mashing at 150°F instead of 152°F to isolate whether that's actually driving the extra fermentability before I start adjusting anything else.

In four decades at the needles I have taught our guild's Fair Isle workshop every autumn, and I still tell newer members it is float tension, not the pattern, that separates a wearable yoke from a puckered one.
I am baking bread every weekend for three months now, I follow the recipe book and not scared of yeast anymore, but my crust is always too pale even when I bake the full time that the book says.

I've finally stopped adding a mystery stitch every row when I purl, so naturally I've decided the next move is a sweater with set-in sleeves, because apparently three scarves in a row wasn't enough humbling.

Let's talk about my shop, because apparently that's the part everyone wants to hear about. I've got a track saw that cost more than my first car, a dust collector with enough suction to reorganize the neighbor's recycling bin, and a benchtop planer I researched for two months before buying. My Instagram followers, all four of them, seem very impressed.

What they don't see is me standing in the garage for twenty minutes trying to remember which way the grain runs before I make a cut, or the pile of 'practice' pocket-hole joints in the scrap bin that are there because my first five attempts split the wood. Last weekend's project was a simple picture ledge, the kind of thing that's basically two boards and a strip of trim, and I still managed to route the rabbet on the wrong edge and have to start the board over.

I watched about six tutorials before I even touched the saw, and I'm still checking a reference chart taped to the wall to remember the difference between a dado and a rabbet, which apparently is a very basic thing to mix up if the comments on my last post are anything to go by. The fancy track saw did make the cut dead straight, I'll give it that, credit where it's due. But straight cuts don't help much when you're not totally sure yet how the joint is supposed to go together in the first place. I'm getting there, slowly, one slightly-too-short board at a time. At least the shop looks professional, even if the guy running it very much is not.

So my neighbor asked why my tomatoes always come in three weeks before hers, and honestly it comes down to years of tweaking — I start seedlings under grow lights in February, harden them off on a schedule taped to the greenhouse door, and I run a soil test every spring so I know exactly what the beds are short on before I amend anything. I save seed from my best-performing plants every year now, so my strain of Brandywine has basically adapted itself to my specific yard. It's not magic, it's just a decade of writing down what worked and what didn't.

okay so I planted the tomatoes like the tag said and watered them basically every day because I figured more water is better right, but now the leaves are all yellow and droopy and I don't get it, my sister said something about them needing 'full sun' but our spot gets shade in the morning so I don't know if that counts or not, and I still can't tell you what the difference between potting soil and garden soil actually is honestly.
I've dialed back my nitrogen feed on the peppers now that they're flowering, since I know from past seasons that too much nitrogen this late just pushes foliage instead of fruit set.

I've been working through Guitar Method Book 2 for about four months now, and I've settled into a practice routine I track pretty carefully: fifteen minutes of chord-switching drills at 60 BPM on the metronome, ten minutes of the songs assigned for the week, and five minutes just noodling to keep it fun. I've got the open chords down cold — G, C, D, Em, Am — and my transitions between them are finally clean enough that a simple song doesn't fall apart every four bars.

Barre chords are where things get interesting. I can hold an F chord for maybe two full strums before my hand cramps up, and my index finger buzzes on the high E string more often than not. I've read that it's mostly about hand position and finger strength rather than brute force, so I've been doing isolated barre drills for five minutes a day separate from regular practice, tracking how many clean strums I get before the buzz starts. Last week it was three strums, this week it's five, so at least the data point is trending the right direction.

I also picked up a cheap capo and I'm slowly working out which songs from my practice list get easier to sing along to when I move the chord shapes up the neck. Still very much in the phase where I have to look at a chord chart taped above my music stand for anything beyond the five chords I've drilled into muscle memory, but the progress feels measurable now instead of random, which helps with the motivation problem more than I expected.

ok so ive been gardening for like 18 years now (started as a kid helping my grandma lol) and these days i run the demo beds at the community garden every spring — teaching the new volunteers succession planting, how to actually read a soil test, all that. still get way too hyped when the first tomatoes come in every year ngl, eighteen years in and it hasn't gotten old.

Quick question for anyone who's dealt with this before — feels dumb to even ask but it's bugging me.

Background on my setup, for context:
- Running the bread program at a 40-seat cafe for going on eleven years now, three ovens, roughly 200 loaves a day between the sourdough country loaf, a rye, and a rotating special
- Hydration on the country loaf sits at 78%, and I adjust it in quarter-percent increments depending on ambient humidity in the bakery, which I log every morning before I start
- I trained two apprentices last year who now run their own small operations, so I'm used to explaining this stuff from scratch when needed

The actual question:
- Starting last month, my usual flour supplier's all-purpose flour has been absorbing noticeably less water than before, maybe half a percent difference, even though the bag still lists the same protein content
- I've ruled out my scale (recalibrated it), my starter (same activity levels, same float test results, same rise timing), and my oven (steam injection timing unchanged)
- Anyone know if mills sometimes shift the protein blend slightly within a stated range without changing the label, or is this more likely a milling date or storage humidity issue on their end?

I know it sounds like a beginner question — "why is my dough acting different" — but I've been chasing consistency on this recipe for over a decade and a half-percent shift is enough to throw off my whole morning bake schedule if I don't catch it early. Just trying to figure out if I need to call the mill or just adjust my formula going forward.

Funny enough, after twenty-some years behind the camera I still get a kick out of mentoring the newer shooters at the co-op — nothing beats watching someone finally get why I keep telling them to meter for the highlights first!

So my coworker Denise has apparently decided that this is the year I get a hobby, because apparently 'doom-scrolling on my lunch break' doesn't count as one, which, fair, but also rude. She's been going on about this for weeks now, ever since the office got that new coffee machine that nobody can figure out how to descale, which is a whole separate saga involving a strongly worded email chain and at least one passive-aggressive sticky note.

Anyway, she showed up on Tuesday with a bag from the craft store and just plopped it on my desk like that settles things. There's yarn in there, some kind of soft blue stuff, and two long sticks that I guess are supposed to be needles, though they don't look anything like sewing needles, which is the only kind of needle I was previously aware existed. I genuinely do not understand why there are two of them. Is that normal? Does something break if you only use one?

Also in the bag was a little booklet that might as well be written in a different language — there are abbreviations everywhere and not one of them is explained anywhere I can find, and a diagram that I think is supposed to show me what to do but mostly just looks like a chart from a math textbook I hated in high school.

Denise says I'll "get the hang of it," which is what she said about the sourdough starter she gave me two years ago that I'm pretty sure is still sitting dead in my fridge. I have exactly zero idea where to even start with these sticks, but I promised her I'd at least look up a video before giving up entirely, so that's this weekend's problem, I guess.

After finally getting my nitrogen cycle to read zero ammonia and zero nitrite for two consecutive weeks, I added my first six neon tetras today, testing the water again this morning just to be extra sure before adding any more.
Lost to a twelve-year-old in a simul yesterday, which is humbling, but at least the three private students I coach on the side paid on time this month, so I'll take the trade.
been doing paid outreach nights at the observatory for a coupla years now, bring my own 10in dob, decent side income even if its not my main job
tried making bread again this weekend and it came out like a brick even though I did the yeast thing and let it sit like the packet said, I don't really get what proofing even means still.
Just wrapped up my third commissioned baby blanket this month — it's wild that people actually pay me for something I used to just do on the couch watching TV!

So this is going to be a bit of a tangent before I get to my actual point, bear with me. My weekend started with my brother-in-law calling me at seven in the morning because his car wouldn't start in my driveway, of all places, and then it turned into this whole thing where we had to jump it three separate times because apparently the battery is basically dead and he just hasn't dealt with it, classic Gary. Anyway, by the time that whole saga wrapped up I'd already missed the farmers market I usually go to on Saturdays, which was annoying because I wanted to grab some of those good peaches before they sold out again like last week.

So I finally got to my actual tanks around noon, which, side note, my youngest daughter has started naming every single fish individually, we're now at forty-one named fish and she gets upset if I mix up which betta is 'Gerald' versus which one is 'Sir Fins-a-Lot,' I did not choose that name, she did.

The reason I was even excited to get to the tanks, though, is that a guy from two towns over reached out because he's setting up his first serious planted tank and wants me to come consult on the hardscape and dosing schedule, paid, which will be my fourth small consulting job this year on top of the fry I sell to the local shop. Not enough to quit my day job by any stretch, but a nice bit of extra income from something I'd be doing anyway.

Anyway, after that I spent the rest of the afternoon trimming stem plants and half-watching a movie with the kids, pretty standard Saturday around here otherwise.

This weekend was very busy for me, not because of fish but because my cousin is visit from overseas and I must show him all around the city, we go to the big market, we eat too much food at the noodle place he like so much, and also his flight was delay four hours so I wait at airport very long time with nothing to do except scroll on phone.

Also my car is making strange noise again, the mechanic say maybe is the belt but he is not sure yet, he want me bring it back next week for look more careful. This is already third time this year something wrong with this car, I think maybe is time for new one but money is tight right now so we will see.

Oh, also for the tank, I finally get comfortable now doing water change every week without checking instruction every time, I know my routine good now. I am working on getting my CO2 dosing more consistent though because my plants still melting little bit when I am not careful with the timing, this is thing I am trying fix for maybe two month now. Other than this I mostly just busy with family stuff this week, cousin leave on Thursday so after that things go back to normal I hope.

Anyway hope everyone have good weekend, mine was tiring but nice to see family even with all the running around.

Hey all! Finally learned how castling actually works last week (still mixing up kingside and queenside half the time, oops) and I'm trying to understand why everyone keeps telling me not to bring my queen out too early — like, isn't she the strongest piece, shouldn't she just go fight? Anyway loving the learning process even when I lose in like ten moves lol.

The through-dovetails on the drawer fronts came out tight enough that I didn't need any glue to hold the joint while I checked the fit, though I'm still not happy with how the pins line up on the back corner.
I got a camera for my birthday and I've been leaving it on whatever mode it came with, since I don't know what half the buttons on top even do yet.
Switched to a two-stage fermentation this batch after reading it helps with clarity, racked to secondary at day ten, still following the timeline from the kit instructions exactly.
My rating's been sitting around 1500 for a few months now, so I've started studying rook endgames specifically since that's clearly where I'm losing the most points.

Finished processing last week's imaging run on the Veil Nebula and wanted to share the workflow, since a few people asked.

Equipment:
- 6-inch f/4 Newtonian astrograph on an EQ6-R Pro mount, guided with a 60mm guide scope and ASI camera
- Dedicated cooled mono camera at -10°C, filter wheel with Ha/OIII/SII narrowband filters
- Polar aligned with a routine that gets me under 30 arcseconds of error before I start

Capture:
- 3 hours of Ha at 300s subs, 2.5 hours of OIII, 2 hours of SII, all from my backyard with a Bortle 6 sky
- Dithering every 4 frames, autofocus triggered every 90 minutes or on a 1.5°C temperature swing
- Guide RMS held under 0.6 arcseconds most of the night, which I'm pretty happy with

Processing:
- Calibrated with darks, flats, and bias frames in the usual stacking software
- Combined in a modified Hubble palette, SII to red, Ha to green, OIII to blue, then rebalanced
- Star reduction and a mild noise reduction pass, tried to keep it restrained rather than overprocessed

Total integration ended up around 7.5 hours, which is more than I usually manage on a single target but the forecast actually cooperated for once. Happy to share the full processing steps if anyone's curious about a specific stage, I've got most of it written down from doing this enough times now that I don't want to forget my own settings.
Finally got the new pedalboard wired during nap time, took a while to get the buffer placement right so the delay trails don't get muddy switching to overdrive mid-song at practice tonight.
I play chess for 25 years now. I coach young players for our national junior team and write endgame articles for a chess magazine.

Quarterly capacity planning wrapped up later than expected this cycle. Facilities moved our floor's server rack allocation without notice, which meant three of the migration windows we'd scheduled for the CRM cutover had to be pushed by a week, and I spent most of Tuesday reconciling the change log with what actually got provisioned versus what the ticket said. The vendor for the new badge readers also missed their install slot twice, so building access on the east wing is still running on the old system, which is its own minor headache for anyone coming in before seven. I did finally get the expense report from my March conference trip approved, four months after submitting it, so that's one fewer red flag in my inbox. On the home front, the 180-gallon SPS reef I've been running has been steady for fourteen months now -- the calcium reactor and the dual-channel dosing pump keep alkalinity within 0.1 dKH of target without me touching anything, and coral growth has been consistent enough that I've started fragging monthly instead of quarterly. Anyway, back to the grind: the migration retro is Thursday, and I still need to pull the incident timeline together before then, plus draft the postmortem template since apparently nobody updated it since the platform switch two years ago. If anyone has a clean postmortem template they don't mind sharing, I'd take it, because rebuilding one from scratch this week is not how I wanted to spend my Wednesday.

Working through my opening repertoire homework this week:
- Reviewed the main lines of the Italian Game and can reach a decent middlegame now
- Still blundering pieces when I try to calculate more than two moves ahead
- Started applying basic pawn structure principles instead of just grabbing material
- Lost twice today by forgetting to check for back-rank threats before castling

This weekend I finish the walnut sideboard that I plan since three months. I use my own jig for the sliding dovetails on the drawers, I build this jig two years ago after first one from magazine plan did not fit good for my shop clamps. The moisture meter say wood is at 7 percent before I start glue up, this is important because last winter I did not check and one panel crack in springtime, now I always wait until reading is stable for one week.

For the finish I mix my own oil and varnish blend, ratio 1:1:1 with mineral spirit, I test on scrap piece first always. The router table I built myself has micro-adjust screw that I add after watching many tutorial, now my dado depth is same every time, not like before when I measure by eye and get small step between passes.

My neighbor ask why I spend so much money on the dust collection system, but with the cyclone separator my shop air is much more clean and I do not cough anymore after long session. I keep log book for every project now, humidity reading, wood movement, glue open time, this help me a lot when something go wrong and I want to know why.

Next project is the curved staircase rail, I already draw the pattern and cut the bending form from MDF. This one will need steam box I have not use before, so I read forum post from other builders first before I try.

I still don't know all the fancy words other bakers use in the forum, but my home steam-injection box and the hydration calculator spreadsheet I made give me the same crumb structure every single bake for over a year now.

Sure, taking on wedding cake orders as a side gig sounded charming until I had a bride call me at 11pm because her venue changed the delivery window. I've got four regular cafes buying my sourdough boules every Saturday now, which is nice for the bank account, though scaling my starter maintenance to match their order volume without babysitting it constantly took longer to figure out than I'd like to admit.
I finally memorized where all six open-position chords sit on the fretboard, but my fingers still won't switch between G and C without a noticeable pause every time.

Camera arrived Tuesday. Body is the entry kit with the 18-55 kit lens, memory card was not included so I ordered a 64GB card separately, arrived Thursday. Battery took three hours to charge fully on first cycle, second charge took two hours ten minutes. Strap that came in the box is too short for my neck so I ordered a replacement, still waiting on that. Weather this week has been overcast, temperature in the low fifties, rain expected Friday and Saturday. I tested the camera in the backyard, then at the park two blocks over, then in the kitchen with the window light. I read the manual section on menu navigation twice. Menu has four tabs, shooting, playback, setup, and custom, each with submenus I have not gone through fully yet. The tripod I ordered separately is a basic aluminum one, ships in five business days according to the tracking page. I also picked up a cleaning cloth and a case, both arrived with the card. None of the photos from the park came out sharp, and I still don't understand what the aperture number on the screen actually controls, so I have been leaving the camera on the green auto mode for everything. Next task is to read the section on shutter speed, then move to aperture once that makes sense. Storage on the card is 64GB, camera writes about 25MB per RAW file according to the spec sheet, so that gives roughly 2,400 shots before the card fills, though I have only used about 40 so far. Plan is to test again this weekend if the rain holds off.

Twenty-two years teaching guitar, currently running four cohorts at the conservatory plus private students on Thursdays. Students ask about scales; I care more about whether their picking hand relaxes under tempo, since that's what separates clean technique from tension injuries later. Industry standard setup specs are a starting point, not a rule -- I adjust action and relief by ear and by the player's callus development.

Wrapping up the review of last month's portrait sessions:
- Calibrated all three studio strobes to match color temperature before the shoot, saved about twenty minutes of correction later
- Switched to a gray card reference shot at the start of each session, white balance is consistent across the whole set now
- Sensor cleaning kit paid for itself this month, caught a dust spot pattern before it showed up on thirty frames
- Still deciding between two macro lenses for the product work, borrowing a copy from a colleague to test first

lol had two apprentices today ask why I still cut my mortises by hand instead of using the domino machine we've got sitting right there. told them once you've done like ten thousand of these your hands just know the depth without measuring, it's the same trick my old shop foreman drilled into me back when I ran the joinery floor at the mill. they didn't believe me till I showed em blind, no gauge, dead on every time

Booked six weekend weddings this fall, on top of my day job. Clients mostly find me through referrals now, which means less time spent on marketing and more on actually editing. My delivery workflow is a culling pass the night of, then color grading in batches over the following week, so I can hand galleries over within ten days without burning out.
barre chords dont trip me up anymore, workin on cleanin up my alternate picking so it doesnt fall apart past 120bpm, used to be way worse lol

Took the telescope out to my uncle's field again last weekend since the light pollution map showed it was way darker out there than my backyard. Finally got Saturn centered without losing it every time I bumped the tripod, which used to drive me nuts, and I'm starting to get a feel for how much the rings actually show depending on the eyepiece I swap in. Still get turned around trying to star-hop from a bright reference star to fainter targets, so I mostly stick to the planets and the Moon for now while I practice with the star charts.
omg so there's this little green sprouty thing poking up in my pot and I have NO idea if it's the thing I planted or just a weed, how do you even tell??

ok so this is my first time EVER trying to make bread and I'm so lost lol. the recipe keeps saying to 'proof' the yeast and I genuinely don't know what that means, I just dumped it in warm water and hoped for the best?? also what's the difference between kneading and just squishing it around, cause that's basically what I did for five minutes before giving up. wish me luck i guess

I acquired a modest refractor some months ago, having decided that retirement afforded ample opportunity to take up a pursuit I had long admired from afar. The instrument came with a star chart and a rudimentary instruction booklet, both of which I have consulted rather more than I anticipated. I have, at least, become tolerably familiar with the terms 'eyepiece' and 'finder scope,' though I confess the latter continues to vex me; no matter how carefully I align it in daylight, by the time darkness falls it seems to have wandered off on its own account, and I spend the better part of an evening merely locating the Moon, which I am given to understand ought to be the simplest of targets. My neighbor, a kind young man with considerably more patience than I possess, attempted to explain the business of 'collimation' to me last week, and I nodded along most agreeably while understanding perhaps a third of it. I did manage, after some persistence, to observe Jupiter on a clear night, though it appeared as little more than a bright, featureless dot, and I am told the bands and moons require both a steadier hand and a good deal more practice than I have yet put in. I have ordered a book on the subject, recommended to me at a local astronomy society meeting I attended as a guest, and I intend to apply myself to it properly before the next clear spell, rather than continuing to fumble about by trial and error as I have done thus far.

Splurged on hand-dyed merino and rosewood needles for this scarf, but still can't tell if I'm doing knit and purl right -- my rows come out uneven and I've lost count of my stitches three times already.

Thursday nights are now officially 'brew night' at the taproom down the street, where I've been running a rotating tap of my saisons and pale ales for about four months, splitting the proceeds with the owner after ingredient costs. Keeping the yeast bank consistent across batches has been the real challenge, since I'm now brewing on a schedule dictated by their pour rate rather than whenever I feel like it, and I've had to start keeping proper batch sheets just to track which starter went into which keg.

After three years of chasing consistency, I finally built a proper temperature-controlled fermentation chamber out of an old chest freezer and an external controller, and the difference in my lagers has been night and day. I'm now hitting the same attenuation within half a percentage point batch after batch, which used to swing all over the place when I was fermenting in the closet with just a space heater and a lot of hope.

I built a RIMS system this spring too, mostly because I got tired of scorching the bottom of my mash tun during longer rests, and the recirculation loop keeps the temperature dead even across the whole grain bed now, no more hot spots throwing off my conversion efficiency. I log every batch in a spreadsheet with strike temperature, mash pH, gravity readings at each stage, and fermentation temperature curves, which sounds excessive until you're trying to figure out why one batch of the same recipe came out half a point higher on final gravity than the last.

Water chemistry has become its own rabbit hole -- I titrate my sparge water now and adjust with lactic acid and calcium chloride depending on the style, since the tap water report changes slightly by season and I got tired of guessing why my hoppy beers sometimes tasted harsher than others. The last twelve batches have all landed within my target range on both gravity and IBU calculations, which is the first time I've felt like I actually understand what's happening in the kettle rather than just following a recipe and hoping.
Bought a starter kit because a friend said it'd be 'easy,' and now I'm googling what 'specific gravity' even means before I've brewed a single batch. Great start.

First time in the shop today:
- Still not sure which end of the tape measure is actually zero
- Cut my board way short because I didn't understand what 'measure twice' was supposed to prevent

Finally got manual mode to feel natural instead of fumbling with the dial mid-shoot, so now I'm just trying to nail focus faster since the toddler won't hold still for more than two seconds at a time.

I set up my very first fish tank this weekend, a lovely little ten-gallon thing from the pet store, and filled it with water straight from the kitchen tap before adding the fish the same afternoon because the box said it was ready to go. Two of them are floating sideways near the top today and I genuinely do not understand what I did wrong, since the water looks perfectly clear to me, and nobody at the store mentioned anything about waiting or testing before adding anyone to the tank.

finally got my tension even enough that I stopped ripping back every other row, which feels like a miracle with a toddler climbing on me mid-stitch, and now I'm just trying to get my cables to lie flatter since they still pucker a little compared to the pattern photos, but honestly compared to where I was six months ago just keeping a straight edge on garter stitch, this feels like real progress even if I know I've still got a long way to go before I'd call anything I make actually polished
Apparently the little horse piece doesn't just move in a straight line like the others, which nobody thought to mention before I lost in four moves to my nephew who is eight.

My neighbor Dana keeps sending new clients my way after I redid her raised beds last spring, so what started as helping one friend for free has somehow turned into four paid garden consults already this month.

I have learned, at some cost to my thumb, that a chisel wants pushing away from oneself, though translating that knowledge into a clean corner on this little box has proven rather more elusive than the instructional pamphlet implied.
